newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: First patient dies under Australian euthanasia.
newsitem.headline: First patient dies under Australian euthanasia.

text.p: An Australian man with prostate cancer has become the first person to die under the world's first law permitting voluntary euthanasia, a doctor in the outback region of the Northern Territory said on Thursday.
The man was killed with a lethal injection.
Dr Philip Nitschke administered the injection at the patient's home in the Northern Territory capital of Darwin.
"A patient has taken advantage of the law and gone ahead and determined to have his life ended last weekend," Nitschke told Australian Broadcasting Corp (ABC) radio.

Nitschke said the patient died on Sunday after medical specialists had signed the necessary paperwork under contoversial assisted-suicide legislation which took effect in the Northern Territory in July.

"On the day elected by the patient he simply indicated to me that he wished to go ahead and I was able to carry out that particular wish of the patient, and things went ahead very smoothly, very well," he said.
Describing the death of the man, Nitschke said it was a "very poignant moment".
"There was also a feeling, of course, that this was the first time ever that a person has been able to legally end their life.
"And there was that sense of history as well," Nitschke said.
The patient had terminal cancer and had been ill for a number of years, the doctor said.

The world's first voluntary euthanasia law was narrowly passed by the Northern Territory legislature but has been bitterly opposed by Australia's leading medical association, right-to-life groups and the Vatican.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard has endorsed moves in the national parliament to overturn the legislation but will allow a conscience vote by politicians.
"It is a matter of principle," Howard said earlier this month. "It goes to the essence of what we see life to be and the sanctity of it and the importance of it and the quality of it."
The territory law allows doctors to help terminally-ill patients kill themselves with a lethal injection or pills.
But until last weekend the law had not been used as doctors were unsure of their legal position in the face of forthcoming High Court and parliamentary challenges.
Euthanasia is illegal in elsewhere in Australia but doctors say it is unofficially practised.
